author: Jack Seale
description:
Can men mend their broken self-esteem with a thicker penis? This documentary about the patients of a Dallas clinic offering PhalloFill® treatment suggests there might be something deeper here

In Bill Moore’s Dallas clinic, every man who drops his pants and lies on the treatment table, braced for the needle, has come looking for something without being sure what it is. As far as their physical selves are concerned, they know exactly what they want, and they are handing over thousands of bucks to pay for it: they all crave a thicker penis. Whether this will mend their broken self-esteem, though, is not clear.

Daniel Lombroso’s documentary about Moore and his patients doesn’t know precisely what it wants either, as it floats between sad stories of modern male self-image that never merge into a singular takeaway argument. Is it about looksmaxxing and the manosphere? At least one participant has picked up questionable ideas from big, bad podcasts, so yes. But the film is als
title: Manhood review – a mind-boggling visit to the penis enlargement doctor who promises ‘better sex than ever’

author: Andrew Roth in Washington
description:
New indictment claims Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in US custody

US federal prosecutors have said that an Iranian operative jailed in New York was responsible for the foiled attack on a UK air force base where American B-1 bombers were stationed.

A new indictment alleged that Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in custody and then transmitted plans – using coded messages in calls to his family – to two co-conspirators to buy large quantities of chemicals that could be used as explosives in an attack on the RAF Fairford base in September.

Continue reading...
title: US prosecutors charge Iranian operative allegedly responsible for UK air force base attack

author: Lucy Mangan
description:
The presenter is an absolute powerhouse – a responsible, clever, ambitious woman without whom nothing and no one around her would survive. So why is she constantly described as bossy?

Stacey Solomon is taking care of five children, 25 chickens, uncountable quail, a large house, a disabled dog and a hugely complicated, successful, busy and lucrative career. Her husband, Joe Swash, is dreaming of a hereditary lake business and adopting an emu.

Everything, in short, is much as it was as the third series of the reality show, Stacey & Joe (this time subtitled In Too Deep), about the nation’s noisiest celebrity couple, begins. Everything is still very loud. Well, Joe is still very loud and thus everyone else still has to strain to be heard over him. Except the cockerel, to whom it comes quite naturally. Joe is afeard of the cockerel. That is because the cockerel clearly hates him. If there ever came a time that the nation was required to choose sides in their war, I would
title: Stacey & Joe: In Too Deep review – Solomon deserves better than these dismal old misogynistic tropes

author: Editorial
description:
Energetic mayors and councils can help street homeless people to rebuild their lives. But the underlying affordability crisis needs tackling too

Bringing an end to rough sleeping was among Andy Burnham’s first pledges after entering Downing Street – as it was when he became mayor of Manchester. With temperatures dropping, and frosts expected, winter night shelters across the UK are up and running. But an ongoing acute shortage of suitable housing and the latest tranche of early prisoner releases mean ministers know that the prime minister’s laudable target is in danger of being missed.

The official figures are shocking. There were 8,748 rough sleepers in England in June, an increa
title: The Guardian view on rough sleeping: Burnham’s laudable target is in danger of being missed | Editorial

author: Arifa Akbar
description:
Hampstead theatre, London
A bickering trio of trapped survivors who have lost their comrades are kept in an ominous stasis in Daisy Bell’s play

The setup is strong in Daisy Hall’s follow-up to her debut, Bellringers. A few survivors on a whaling ship trapped in arctic ice are figuring out how to break free as the ice groans and explodes ominously around them.

Babben (Justin Edwards) is an old hand who has whaled for almost 40 years; Gorey (Adam Rojko Vega) is a mischief-maker who walks around with a gun; the youngest, and most strait-laced, is Sam (Abdul Jalloh) who seems immobilised by anxiety.

Continue reading...
title: There’s scurvy, mutiny and mystery in Dogstar – but like its icebound ship this drama goes nowhere

author: Jacob Steinberg
description:
Fearless winger has forced his way into Thomas Tuchel’s plans and believes he can become best player in the world

Rio Ngumoha is fearless, exciting and ready to make his mark as an England player. The Liverpool winger narrowly missed the cut for the World Cup squad last summer but he impressed during the pre-tournament camp in Florida and has forced his way into Thomas Tuchel’s plans after an excellent start to the season.

There is an opportunity for the 18-year-old to advance his case with Bukayo Saka injured and more experienced players left out for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain this week. Ngumoha, who is dangerous on both flanks, has a chance of starting when Croatia visit Wembley on Thursday and would love to test himself against Lamine Yamal when England face Spain in Madrid on Sunday.
title: Rio Ngumoha ready to make England splash as he spells out Ballon d’Or ambition

author: Guardian Staff
description:
More than half of Paraguay’s population woke up on 3 November unable to access their bank accounts. It was a day after payday, and Ueno - a bank that expanded exponentially under Santiago Peña's government - found itself at the centre of a political and economic crisis that brought the country’s banking system to the brink of collapse. Protests spread across the country, some involving violent clashes with police. Impeachment proceedings began, and on 6 November Paraguay's rightwing president was impeached and placed under house arrest

  • ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke

  • Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking c
title: How Paraguay's banking crisis ousted a president and left millions broke – explainer

author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya
description:
António Guterres calls for ‘clear next steps’ as countries face pressure to agree concrete measures

Turkey and Australia, the co-hosts of crucial climate talks, must urgently move from discussing the end of fossil fuels to delivering it, the UN chief has said.

“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday. “Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.”

Continue reading...
title: UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action

author: Guardian Staff
description:
The key task should be to ensure that essential services improve the wellbeing of individuals and local communities, writes Peter Riddle. Plus letters from Sheila Triggs and Stephen Smith

A key lesson for the UK from the US midterm elections is that a different approach to managing the economy is essential if Labour hopes to retain power in two years’ time. Voters in the UK will judge Andy Burnham’s government just as harshly as American voters have judged Donald Trump if they too feel the economy is not working for them.

Meeting the rising costs of food, utilities, transport and housing has become a daily challenge for millions of people. The pain of rising costs is compounded by a collapse in the quality and reliability of many vital public services and a sense that many people feel that their community life has become more fractious, fragile and unsafe.
title: Growth at all costs is not a sustainable policy | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Vicky Wolmuth says the subsidy is unfair to British students, but Moira Hankinson writes that it would offer employers students with a wider outlook

I was appalled to read that the government is planning to subsidise EU students studying at UK universities (UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme, 1 November).

My daughters are both on Plan 2 student loan repayment schemes, with their crippling accumulative 9% interest rates deducted at source from their salaries. The student Plan 2 loan scheme has become a financial burden for those graduates for the next 30 years. Getting a foot on the housing ladder in London, with the high cost of
title: Is it fair to give EU students discounted university fees in the UK? | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Mark Bergfeld suggests the quest for a better quality of life deserves as much political recognition as climbing a career ladder

Gaby Hinsliff’s portrait of Claire Ainsley and her latest book Control: How We Lost It and How to Take It Back (‘The world is out of control’: how political strategist Claire Ainsley is challenging the left to take it back, 3 November) leaves a crucial question unanswered: can working people exercise control collectively over those in power?

Reviewing her earlier book The New Working Class for the Global Labour Journal in 2020, I argued that she treated working-class people primarily as voters to be won over rather than people capable of organising to change society.
title: A proper leftwing take on taking back control | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article by John Harris in which he argues that around the world virtues such as kindness and compassion are gathering dust

John Harris’s powerful article exposes the growing assault on empathy in politics (From the US midterms to the hard right in Britain, empathy has become a dirty word in politics, 3 November). But why has empathy become such a threatening quality? Perhaps because extinguishing it completes the work of aggressive neoliberalism by severing the last thread of the social contract: our sense of responsibility for one another. If we can persuade ourselves that people are to blame for their own suffering, and that helping them merely enables dependency, we can abandon them without guilt.

We founded Compassion in Politics in the aftermath of Brexit and Trump’s first elect
title: Compassion is the antidote to the politics of cruelty | Letters

author: John Crace
description:
The Tory leader outlines her £36bn welfare cuts, again, to an audience of an age and a wealth that they don’t need to work

Call it tough love. Only without any of the love bit. Let’s face it. There comes a time in every Conservative politician’s life when you have to say enough is enough. That it’s just not fair on the rest of us. Now, MPs might just have enjoyed a five-day mini-recess, but they deserve every minute’s free time they get. Because they clearly work far harder than everyone else. But on a Tuesday morning it sticks in the throat to think of people lying around at home, being paid to have disabilities that exist mainly in their imaginations, while you have to give a speech in central London.

The thing is, we just haven’t been ambitious enough for people on welfare payments. Let me introduce you to KemiWorld. Think of the double amputee who ran a marathon. Though try not to think of the cost to the NHS of the prosthetics. Welfare is very much a one-way balanc
title: Call it tough love, with the love removed: it’s Kemi’s war on benefits claimants

author: Oliver Wainwright
description:
Ruggedly good-looking and greener than bricks and concrete, Petra Heights are made of three-metre slabs of rough rock. Could they herald a new stone age? Our writer fires up his Flintmobile

There’s been a geological eruption on London’s Finchley Road. Great chunks of pink basalt and igneous larvikite appear to have exploded from the railway cutting, shooting skywards to form teetering towers. Anyone trying to find Finchley Road & Frognal station need wonder no more: just look for the multistorey Stonehenge.

Countless apartment towers have sprouted above London’s stations in recent years, a result of public transport-oriented policies, but none have looked like the Flintstones were in charge.

Continue reading...
title: Yabba dabba doo! Could these bulging, Flintstones-style towers be the future of eco-building?

author: Graeme Wearden
description:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

  • Nvidia and Jensen Huang sued by shareholders over affair with alleged Chinese spy

  • The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security

  • Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?

A senior US central banker is calling for a hike in interest rates next month.

Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller is arguing that the Fed should raise short-term borrowing costs next month even if government data shows inflation cooling.

“While I am hoping for an impr
title: Bank of England’s Lombardelli warns UK’s ‘low-hire, low-fire’ labour market hurting young people – business live

author: Leslie Felperin
description:
Director Vincent Munier takes his father and son into the Vosges forest in France and finds lynx, serene foxes and deer

Cannily timed to overlap but also contrast with the BBC’s Blue Planet III, this French nature documentary embodies a very different way to go about things. Instead of the detached, friendly style of David Attenborough with his generous sprinkle of zoological facts and figures, Whispers in the Woods is a more emotionally driven, visually stylised work that emphasises the interaction of the human and the animal realm.

Its director, Vincent Munier, previously made The Velvet Queen, a swooning study of his and writer Sylvain Tesson’s search for snow leopards in Tibet. This time round, Munier places his father Michael, a naturalist, and his own teenage son Simon at the centre of the action; we experience the film largely through Simon’s br
title: Whispers in the Woods review – paddling in the moonlight in tender study of human-animal interaction

author: Chris Wiegand Stage editor
description:
Rupert Goold begins his tenure as artistic director with a ‘provocative’ version of Shakespeare’s history play, followed by shows starring Milly Alcock and Arinzé Kene

Damian Lewis is to play Henry V at the Old Vic in London in the first production under the theatre’s new artistic director, Rupert Goold.

Goold will direct what is billed as a “provocative” version of Shakespeare’s history play that challenges “what makes a leader a legend”. It will be Lewis’s first major theatre role since he starred in The Goat, or Who Is Sylvia? almost 10 years ago. He has previously played Romeo and Hamlet on stage, as well as appearing in Cymbeline and Much Ado About Nothing for the Royal Shakespeare Company.

Continue reading...
title: Old Vic 2027 season to open with Damian Lewis as Henry V

author: Moira Donegan
description:
The potential presidential contender has misread the electorate – and that’s just the start of his problems

The good news is that the dramatic results of last week’s midterm elections mean that Donald Trump and his administration will be much less able to immiserate and impoverish the American people for the next two years, that newly competitive states are likely to see an influx of investment from Democrats, and that states that were once under seemingly unbreakable regimes of Republican control now have Democratic state governments that will hopefully pursue more just, or at least less cruel, policy agendas.

The bad news is that the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.

Continue reading...
title: JD Vance’s first 2028 pitch reveals his profound weakness as a candidate | Moira Donegan

author: Michael Savage Media editor
description:
Effort to stop Guardian and ITN from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual behaviour was unprecedented

  • Revealed: David Walliams accused of using celebrity status to prey on young women for sex

  • Read the full investigation: ‘It wasn’t long until he asked me if I’d ever had sex before’

The high court attempt by David Walliams to stop the Guardian and ITN from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual behaviour was unprecedented. Here are the key issues surrounding the case.

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in
title: What are the key legal issues surrounding the David Walliams case?

author: Chris Stein in Washington
description:
With weeks left on the congressional calendar, House and Senate representatives have a host of issues they still need to tackle

On their first day back in the Capitol after comprehensive defeats in last week’s midterm elections, Republicans were divided into two camps: those who saw the catastrophe coming, and those who did not.

“I told you exactly what was going to happen. Over and over and over, I told you,” said West Virginia senator Jim Justice. “I said really and truly, if you weren’t concerned and you were a Republican, you were living in a cave. That was my exact words.”

Continue reading...
title: Republicans return to Washington to sift through wreckage of midterms rout

author: Guardian community team
description:
We’d like to hear from retail workers about their experiences of abuse, threats and violence at work

More than half of UK shop workers face abuse or attacks from customers every week, according to new research by the charity Retail Trust. The figure has risen from 33% to 54% in just two years, prompting calls for shoppers to show greater respect ahead of the upcoming busy Christmas period.

We’d like to hear from retail workers about their experiences. Have you faced verbal abuse, threats or physical violence from customers or have you been filmed without your consent?

Continue
title: Shop workers in the UK: have you experienced abuse from customers?

author: Leon Poultney
description:
Want to get your steps in while working or watching TV? Our expert puts walking pads through their paces to find the best for comfort, noise and ease of storage

• The best treadmills for your home

You don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15%.

However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing mor
title: Are walking pads worth it? We put the best under-desk treadmills to the test

author: Rupert Jones
description:
Joining a company scheme at 18 seemed ‘too expensive’ for Rio until someone close put him right

One 20-year-old’s financial future is looking brighter after his aunt convinced him to join his workplace pension and take advantage of the “free money” on offer.

Rio started working at 18, too young to be “auto-enrolled” into his company’s pension scheme. He as given the option to join but had decided not to because he felt it was too expensive – but, fortunately for him, his “Auntie Susan” is a pensions expert at a leading retirement firm, and she soon put him right.

Continue reading...
title: How a chat with ‘auntie’ helped a young worker bag free money in a UK pensions scheme

author: Phil Harrison, Ali Catterall and Hannah J Davies
description:
A nonjudgemental look at looksmaxxing and male insecurity. Plus, what’s really happening in the lives of Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash? Here’s what to watch this evening

10pm, BBC Four

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: a documentary about penis enhancement surgery

author: Ed Douglas
description:
South Yorkshire: It’s the river that gave the city its name, and for the first time in 160 years train passengers can catch a glimpse beneath their feet

The ground under my feet starts vibrating, so I look up and see a London train rumbling into view. Two crows, also disturbed, lift themselves off a signalling mast to settle again on a high wall dotted with buddleia. A few gulls are squabbling overhead against a greying sky that has left Platform 5A slick with drizzle. Then I lower my head again to the mesmerising square of water rushing beneath my feet.

It is the first view of the River Sheaf at this spot since the late 1860s, when it was culverted and plunged into darkness for the construction of Sheffield station, right where another stream, the Porter Brook, flows into it. Now, like some Roman mosaic or Anglo-Saxon hoard, a fragment of this treasure has been exposed, with the opening of a lightwell, protected by a steel grille, that allows rail
title: Country diary: Lost and found at Sheffield station – a section of the River Sheaf | Ed Douglas

author: Jack Snape
description:
• No ‘compelling reason’ to establish another inquiry into incident

  • Usman Khawaja says ‘this has never been about commercial gain’

Cricket Australia will not reopen the investigation into the 2018 ball tampering controversy reignited by the release this week of Usman Khawaja’s book, which alleged more than the three players suspended had knowledge of the sandpaper plan.

Captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were handed long bans following a short Cricket Australia investigation into the incident.

Continue reading...
title: Cricket Australia rules out reopening ball tampering investigation in wake of Khawaja book claims

author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
description:
However, authors of a comprehensive assessment to be presented at Cop31 warn talk of a global turnaround premature

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.
title: Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push
